description: Gem Match online free: swap neighbouring gems to match three or more in a row. 60 seconds on the clock — every match scores, and chain reactions multiply the points.
lede: Six colours, six shapes, sixty seconds. Swap two neighbouring gems to line up three or more of a kind and they pop, the gems above drop down, and new ones fall in — and if those make a match of their own, the points multiply. It is the simplest rule in puzzle games and the hardest to put down: one more swap, one more chain, one more best score.

p: Press Play and the clock starts: 60 seconds. Click a gem, then click a neighbour to swap them — or just drag a gem in the direction you want it to go. If the swap lines up three or more gems of the same colour in a row or a column, they clear and you score. If it makes no match, the gems swap straight back, so a wrong guess costs you nothing but a moment.

Matched gems disappear and everything above drops down, which often lines up a second match all by itself. Those chain reactions — cascades — multiply your points, so a lucky board can turn one swap into a run of clears. When the timer hits zero, your score is final.

Every gem you clear is worth 10 points, multiplied by the cascade it belongs to: the first match of a swap scores at ×1, a chain reaction that follows it scores at ×2, the next at ×3, and so on. Longer matches clear more gems at once, so a four-in-a-row scores more than a three-in-a-row — and setting up a cascade is worth far more than grabbing the first match you see.
There is no penalty for a swap that matches nothing, and no limit on hints: the Hint button always shows a swap that works. The only thing that runs out is time, so spend it matching, not staring.

p: The match-three idea is older than the smartphone: Shariki, a 1994 DOS game, had players swapping gems on a grid, but it was Bejeweled, released by PopCap Games in 2001, that turned swapping gems into one of the most played puzzle formats in the world. Its rule was exactly this one — swap neighbours, match three, watch them pop.

Candy Crush Saga, launched by King in 2012, put the same idea on phones with a timer, a move limit and a map of hundreds of levels, and became one of the highest-grossing mobile games ever made. This version keeps the original spirit: one board, one minute, and the score is all that matters.

ol: Look for the cascade, not the match. A swap that drops gems into a second match is worth double, and a third is worth triple.
Match at the bottom of the board first. Gems fall from the top, so a low match shakes up more of the board than a high one.
A four-in-a-row clears four gems and often starts a cascade — it is almost always worth more than two separate threes.
Use the Hint button when the board looks dead. It finds a working swap in a blink, and there is no penalty for using it.
When fewer than 15 seconds are left, stop hunting for cascades and grab every match you can see — a small match banked beats a big one you never make.

p: If you like sliding tiles instead of swapping gems, chase the 2048 tile in [[2048]]. For a calmer matching game with no timer at all, turn over pairs in [[memory-match]]. You can find every puzzle in [[cat:puzzle|puzzle games]].

faq: What happens if my swap makes no match?
Nothing bad. The two gems swap straight back, your score does not change, and the clock keeps running. There is no penalty for a wrong guess.
When cleared gems drop new ones into place and those make a match by themselves. The first match of a swap scores at ×1, the cascade that follows at ×2, then ×3, and so on.
What if there are no moves left?
The board shuffles itself automatically and play continues — you never get stuck with a dead board.
